11.0.0.en: Nahash the Ammonite: The Ammonites and the Moabites were descendants of Lot and lived east of the Jordan River, and their land became the portion of the tribe of Gad together with Reuben and half the tribe of Manasseh. They had wars with the people of Israel, such as what happened in the time of the Judges (Judg 11:5), when Jephthah the Gileadite defeated them. Their king was called Nahash, and the meaning of his name is “serpent,” that is, a snake.

11.0.1.en: Jabesh-gilead: One of the cities of the tribe of Gad, located on Mount Gilead east of the Jordan River. It seems that it had a relationship with the tribe of Benjamin, so that its people did not join the rest of the tribes in disciplining the tribe of Benjamin when it sinned. For this reason the tribes attacked the city of Jabesh, killed many of its people and destroyed the city (Judg 21:10). Jabesh-gilead: it is a city on Mount Gilead east of the Jordan River.

11.0.2.en: Shortly after Saul began to reign (and the Septuagint mentions that it was after a month), Nahash king of the Ammonites made a raid in which he prevailed over the people of the cities of Jabesh-gilead. When the people of the city feared that he would kill them, they asked him for a covenant and a promise that he would let them go their way, and they were ready to become his servants all the days of their lives.

11.0.3.en: There is another opinion, mentioned in (ch. 12:12), that the people of Jabesh asked for a king to repel Nahash from them, so God chose Saul as king for them by the hand of Samuel. This does not contradict what is said in this verse, because Nahash may have made earlier raids on Jabesh months before, on account of which they asked for a king; and after Saul was anointed, Nahash rose up to seize the city and kill those in it, so here they called for help upon Saul, who had been anointed about a month before.

11.1.0.en: In the pride and arrogance of the conqueror, Nahash king of Ammon answered that he was ready to make a covenant with them not to kill them, namely that he would put out the right eye of all the people of the city, so that this would be a disgrace and a reproach not only to the people of Jabesh-gilead but to all the people of Israel.

11.1.1.en: Putting out the eyes was a well-known humiliation among the pagans in ancient times, as the Philistines did to Samson (Judg 16:21) and as Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon later did to Zedekiah king of Judah (2 Kgs 25:7). For putting out the right eye made men unable to fight, because the warrior carried the shield in his left hand to protect his face and body with it, yet he could at least see with his right eye; but if that eye was put out, it became very difficult for him to fight, because if he protected himself with the shield he could not see his enemy, and if he did not protect himself with the shield he became exposed to the enemy’s arrows.

11.1.2.en: Putting out the eyes is a symbol of a person losing his spiritual sight, and this is what Satan tries to do to the children of God.

11.2.0.en: Faced with this ordeal and this hard demand, the inhabitants of Jabesh did not know what to do, so their elders came out with a proposal to Nahash king of the Ammonites: that he give them a respite of one week to seek help from all the tribes, and if no one responded to rescue them, they would come out to him, meaning they would surrender themselves to him to do with them what he wished. Nahash agreed, being certain that no one would dare to support them for fear of him, for his arrogance made him sure of his strength. And so, in the end, because of the threats and cruelty of Nahash, they asked for a respite in order to take refuge in God and to seek the help of Saul their king. It would have been better for them not to accept slavery to Nahash, even if he were not going to put out their eyes, but to pray to God and ask the help of their king.

11.3.0.en: Indeed, the people of the city sent their messengers to the place where Saul lived and told what had happened to them, and everyone was moved and wept for their brothers. As for Saul, who was not yet a king in the accepted sense and had no retinue or the like, he was carrying out his daily work of plowing the land to sow it or tending the cattle by feeding them the grass of the field. On his return he heard the cries and weeping of the people, and when he asked them the reason, they told him what they had heard about the story of the people of Jabesh.

11.3.1.en: We notice that Saul was still afraid of his new position as king and still carried on his ordinary work of tending the cattle.

11.4.0.en: Saul became very angry when he heard this story, and the expression “the Spirit of God came upon him” is so that we may know that it was a holy anger, according to God’s purpose, and not merely a human emotion.

11.5.0.en: A yoke of oxen: a pair of oxen.

11.5.1.en: Saul took a pair of oxen, slaughtered them and cut them into pieces, and sent the messengers to all the tribes carrying these cut-up oxen. There was a clear and decisive message directed to all, which was that whoever held back from answering the call and going out to war behind Saul and Samuel would have as his punishment that Saul would tear his oxen apart as he had slaughtered and torn apart these oxen. This message, together with the sight of the torn oxen, had a fearful effect on the people in every direction, so all the Jews went out behind Saul as one man.

11.5.2.en: His mention of “after Saul and after Samuel” shows his faith that the war belonged to God, whom His prophet Samuel represented. It shows his submission to God and to Samuel.

11.5.3.en: Perhaps Saul cut up the oxen in this way in imitation of what the Levite did with his concubine (Judg 20:6). Saul was gentle at the beginning of his reign, for he did not declare that he would kill every person who did not go out with him to war, but only that he would slaughter his oxen.

11.6.0.en: Bezek: a city located in the portion of the tribe of Judah.

11.6.1.en: The men of the children of Israel gathered for war, from twenty years old and upward, in the town of “Bezek,” and Saul numbered them as the commander of the war; and three hundred thousand men came out from the eleven tribes. The number of the tribe of Judah is given as thirty thousand because it is smaller than would be expected of the tribe of Judah, which was one of the largest tribes in number at that time. Perhaps this was because of the pride of the tribe of Judah and their distress that the king was not taken from their tribe but from the tribe of Benjamin.

11.7.0.en: We understand from this verse that the messengers whom the people of “Jabesh-gilead” had sent did not leave Gibeah of Saul, awaiting his reply. When this vast number of Israel had gathered, Saul gave a reassuring reply to the people of “Jabesh,” saying to them that by the time the day grew hot they would have deliverance and victory over the Ammonites and over their king. When this good news reached the people of Jabesh, they rejoiced greatly that Israel had responded to their cry for help. After this they sent messengers to Nahash king of the Ammonites, who had given them a respite of a week, and said, “Tomorrow we will come out to you, and you shall do with us all that seems good to you.” This was a kind of camouflage and deception in war, for the children of Israel attacked him before that time while he was not prepared for battle.

11.7.1.en: God gave Saul the opportunity to establish his kingdom and lead the people in war. So do not be careless when God gives you an opportunity to prove your love for Him; that is, seize every spiritual opportunity to draw near to Him, and when distress meets you, hasten to Him to declare your repentance to Him and receive His strength and His blessings.

11.8.s.en: (2) Saul’s victory and the establishment of his kingdom

11.8.0.en: The morning watch: very early morning.

11.8.1.en: The heat of the day: the intensifying of the sun, which is the time from noon until three in the afternoon.

11.8.2.en: Although Saul was a farmer who knew nothing of the affairs of war, yet because God was with him we find him thinking like a seasoned commander and dividing the number of men into three companies. He surprised the camp of the Ammonites before dawn, and they kept striking and fighting the Ammonites with strength until the sun grew hot. The victory of Israel was great, for the Ammonites fled and were scattered, each in a different direction to save himself. The people of Jabesh-gilead rejoiced more than all the children of Israel because God delivered them by the hand of Saul, and they kept this kindness for Saul even after his death: they took down his body and the bodies of his sons when the Philistines hung them up to put them to shame, and they buried them, and David praised their deed (ch. 31:11-13, 2 Sam 2:4-7). Thus this ordeal showed the strength and wisdom of Saul which God had given him, and he became king officially and won the confidence of the people after his victory over the Ammonites. So do not fear temptation, for it may be your road to glory by the ordering of God.

11.9.0.en: The victorious people gathered, greatly rejoicing in their king Saul, the leader of the war. In the exhilaration of this victory, and either to flatter Saul or out of sincere feelings of love for him, they asked Samuel, who was still regarded as the spiritual leader of the people, to bring the men who had rejected Saul as king over the people, and who had earlier been described as “sons of Belial” (ch. 10:27), in order to put them to death, since they regarded them as traitors to the new king who had disobeyed God’s command in appointing Saul king.

11.10.0.en: But Saul showed wisdom, love and forbearance when he did not listen to them, and his answer was sober. He directed the people’s attention to the fact that this day was a day of rejoicing in God’s victory for them over the enemies, so it was more fitting that they offer in it thanksgiving, praise and glorification to the name of God rather than that blood be shed in it and it become a sorrow in Israel, at least to the families of those men.

11.10.1.en: It is good for a leader, a priest or a servant to be merciful to those who oppose him or are hostile to him, however wrong they may be, and to be long-suffering toward them, so that perhaps he may bring them back to God by love and persuasion instead of taking vengeance for himself by exploiting his authority.

11.11.0.en: Gilgal: a city near Jericho which Joshua took as his center for leading the people.

11.11.1.en: We have said before that Gilgal was a spiritual and political center for the people. When Samuel saw that the people were gathered around Saul and rejoiced in him, he too rejoiced and took advantage of this opportunity and called the people to go to Gilgal to renew the kingdom. The meaning is that he used this victory to establish Saul in the kingdom, or, as we say in political language these days, “we pledge allegiance to so-and-so” ... that is, the pledging of allegiance to Saul as king over all the tribes.

11.12.0.en: Peace offerings: sacrifices of thanksgiving to God in which those who offer them share in eating of them.

11.12.1.en: The people’s celebration of Saul at Gilgal is considered his real coronation and the beginning of the establishment of his kingdom after his victory and the rallying of the men around him. Among the features of that celebration were the offering of sacrifices to thank the Lord for His deed and His deliverance, and other festivities that were a cause of gladness to the heart of Saul and all the people of Israel. A long address by Samuel to the people

12.0.0.en: Samuel begins his address to the people by explaining to them that he had responded to what they asked, setting a king over them, even though this involved a rejection of God and of Samuel’s leadership.

12.1.0.en: “And now you have this king who goes before you and leads you; as for me, my task as the last judge of Israel comes to an end. I was a spiritual leader and a judge to you from the years of my early youth until now, and I have grown old and my hair is gray, and my sons will be with you.” His words “behold, my sons are with you” have two interpretations:

12.1.1.en: 1- Either Samuel had removed them because of their bad conduct, so “with you” means that they had become like the rest of the people, and the king alone has the authority of ruling and judging.

12.1.2.en: 2- Samuel did not remove them but rebuked them and left them with the people under the rule of the new king, who has the right to supervise them and confirm them if they judge rightly or remove them if they err, for the king has authority over them like his authority over the rest of the people.

12.2.1.en: Hide my eyes: not look; the meaning is being lenient with the wicked and leaving them to do evil in return for a material reward.

12.2.2.en: Samuel declared his innocence of seizing the livestock or possessions of anyone among the people, or of taking a bribe to be lenient with the wicked, or of wronging anyone. He said this before the people and in the presence of the anointed king Saul.

12.3.0.en: The answer of the people came as Samuel expected, for they testified to his justice and integrity, and that he had not wronged anyone in anything, had not oppressed anyone in anything, and had taken nothing from anyone’s hand.

12.4.0.en: Despite the people’s acknowledgment of his integrity, Samuel was not content with this but wanted God also to enter as a witness, and Saul as well. So he repeated to them that God is witness to what they had said, and Saul is also witness to what he had heard from them, and they answered, confirming: “Yes, God is witness to what we have said.”

12.4.1.en: By this Samuel declared his innocence in his shepherding of the people, as Christ did when He said to the people, “Which of you convinceth me of sin?” (Jn 8:46). By this he is an example to the king, the leaders and all the people in their conduct with others. And as the Apostle Paul said, “Be ye followers of me, even as I also am of Christ” (1 Cor 11:1). By this Samuel declares three things:

12.4.2.en: 1- The end of his political work and his work as a judge, so as to devote himself to spiritual guidance and leave the ruling to the king.

12.4.3.en: 2- The declaration of his integrity, to be an example to the new king.

12.4.4.en: 3- The declaration of his integrity helps him in warning the people as a spiritual guide who is responsible for them before God, and a warning is accepted only from an upright person.

12.4.5.en: He will declare this warning in the following verses.

12.4.6.en: Be pure in carrying out your responsibilities for the sake of God, who sees everything and will reward you and bless you. Do not cause anyone to stumble for the sake of passing things, and do not flatter anyone at the expense of the truth, or out of fear of him or out of shyness.

12.5.s.en: (2) God’s care and warning them against opposing Him

12.5.0.en: One of the beautiful and recurring pictures is that when a man of God wants to speak to the people, he begins first by reviewing God’s work with the people before addressing his personal words to them. So did Moses and Joshua, and also Peter and Stephen (the Book of Acts). Here we see Samuel reviewing with the people God’s power and His care for them: when the humiliation increased in the land of Egypt, He raised up for them Moses and Aaron, who led the people and brought them out of the land of Egypt.

12.6.0.en: The righteous acts of the Lord: His care and His works with His people.

12.6.1.en: “Now therefore, O people, come forward and stand before God, that you may be reckoned with before Him and before all His mighty works with you and with your fathers of old. When Jacob and his sons went down to the land of Egypt and stayed there many years, they multiplied in it, and Pharaoh made them slaves to him and humiliated them. Did not God bring out for you Moses and Aaron, who led the people in the wilderness for forty years, and afterward God settled you in this land which you have possessed?”

12.7.0.en: Hazor: the name of a Canaanite city.

12.7.1.en: “But your fathers disobeyed God and did not keep His covenant and served other gods, so the Lord left them to the hand of Sisera the Canaanite to humble them, and likewise He left them to the hand of the Philistines to weary and oppress them in the land, and likewise He let the Moabites loose on them, and they fought them, and there were no days of rest for our people!”

12.8.0.en: Jerubbaal: Gideon (Judg 7:1). Bedan: he is Barak, or Samson, or another judge who is not mentioned in the Book of Judges.

12.8.1.en: Whenever they were defeated before the enemies of the land, they cried out to God, asking forgiveness for having forsaken Him and worshiped Baal and his wife Ashtoreth (from the gods of the pagan nations). Each time God had compassion on His people and sent them judges such as Gideon and Bedan, and likewise He sent them Jephthah and Samuel, who delivered them from their enemies who had oppressed them.

12.9.0.en: And after all of God’s previous work with them, when Nahash king of the children of Ammon came upon them and besieged them and prevailed over them, instead of crying out to God to deliver them, they asked for a king from among men, like the rest of the peoples, to deliver them, and they replaced God with him.

12.10.0.en: “And here now God has responded to you and given you a king according to your choice. If you walk in the fear of God and serve Him, and do not take gods from the nations to worship them, and listen to His voice and His commandments and do not disobey any command of His, but you and the chosen king follow Him with all your hearts, then of course God will be with you and will bless the people and their king.

12.11.0.en: But if you do not listen to the voice of the Lord, and go after what angers Him and disobey His command, the hand of the Lord will be against you, and He will avenge Himself for your evil and allow your enemies to rule over you and humble you, exactly as it was with your fathers when they turned aside from God.”

12.11.1.en: God stretches out His hand to you in love and is ready to keep you and care for you, on condition that you hold fast to your sonship to Him and keep His commandments. But if you become preoccupied with the world and attached to its material things, God will forsake you, and the evils and troubles of the world will crush you.

12.12.0.en: After Samuel finished part of his address, he asked all the people to stand attentively before God, because he was about to ask the Lord for a sign before the eyes of the people, to confirm to them their error when they chose for themselves an earthly king instead of God, their true King.

12.13.0.en: Samuel asked God to show His glory by working a miracle, which was the coming forth of thunder and the falling of rain at the time of the wheat harvest, which is the month of May, when the hot weather begins and the rains end in this region. This was so that the people would know their evil in asking for an earthly king instead of God their true King, and so that they would fear God, their true King, who is able to do all things, before they feared the earthly king Saul, who is an instrument in God’s hand. Thus they would realize their evil in replacing God, who is almighty, with a man limited in his abilities, and would understand that if they and the king submit to God, He will not forsake them but will bless them.

12.14.0.en: When Samuel asked God to show His glory, the people heard mighty thunder and the rain fell at once, so the people feared God and felt the greatness of their sin. They also feared Samuel, for they felt that he was the mighty man of God whose word the heavens carry out at once, so the thunder comes forth and the rains fall. On the other hand, they became aware that God is their true King and not this anointed king.

12.14.1.en: Beloved brother, this lesson is for all of us, for we often replace God and rely on people and acquaintances to help us in managing our affairs ... Turn to God first, and He will guide you to whom you should go and how the matter will be settled for you, and do not forget that God cursed the one who trusts in the arm of man.

12.15.0.en: In front of this miracle and this wonderful event, the people stood before Samuel the prophet, asking him for intercession and prayer for their sin which they had committed, so that God would not destroy them from before Him, and they confessed their pride when they asked a king for themselves.

12.16.0.en: Samuel reassured his frightened people that God would not destroy them, since He is long-suffering, but on condition that they hold fast to His commandments and not imitate the nations by worshiping idols, which profit nothing, for they had asked for a king to be like the pagan nations around them.

12.17.0.en: Samuel explained the reason God does not destroy them, which is that He wants them to be His people, and for the sake of His holy name He will keep them, not because of their goodness, giving them an opportunity to repent. For He wants to make His name known among the nations through His people, therefore He is long-suffering toward them despite their sins.

12.18.0.en: “As for me, Samuel, far be it from me that I should neglect to pray for you.” The meaning of this is that he will not cease praying for his people, and he considered not praying for them a sin before God, and for this reason he used the expression “far be it.” “And I will not stop at praying for you only, but I will also not cease teaching and directing you to everything that is good and right before God.”

12.19.0.en: “And you must set God before your eyes, and serve Him with all faithfulness and care and with pure hearts, and not with the worship of the tongue, and meditate on all His works, past and present, by which He has repeatedly raised you from your humiliation before your enemies.”

12.20.0.en: Samuel warned them not to return to their evils, lest God destroy them and their king.

12.20.1.en: Take care to pray for those around you, especially when you see some committing obvious sins. Do not condemn them, but know that God has allowed you to see these sins so that you may pray much for them, and God will rejoice in your love for them and lift their sins from them, and you will grow in the love of God and receive His blessings.

12.20.2.en: Preparation for fighting the Philistines (1) Saul prepares an army and offers a burnt offering to the Lord (vv. 1-9): 1 Saul was one year old in his kingdom, and he reigned two years over Israel. 2 And Saul chose for himself three thousand men of Israel, of which two thousand were with Saul in Michmash and in mount Bethel, and a thousand were with Jonathan in Gibeah of Benjamin: and the rest of the people he sent every man to his tent. 3 And Jonathan smote the garrison of the Philistines that was in Geba, and the Philistines heard of it. And Saul blew the trumpet throughout all the land, saying, Let the Hebrews hear. 4 And all Israel heard say that Saul had smitten a garrison of the Philistines, and that Israel also was had in abomination with the Philistines. And the people were called together after Saul to Gilgal. 5 And the Philistines gathered themselves together to fight with Israel, thirty thousand chariots, and six thousand horsemen, and people as the sand which is on the sea shore in multitude: and they came up, and pitched in Michmash, eastward from Beth-aven. 6 When the men of Israel saw that they were in a strait, the people hid themselves in caves, and in thickets, and in rocks, and in high places, and in pits. 7 And some of the Hebrews went over Jordan to the land of Gad and Gilead. As for Saul, he was yet in Gilgal, and all the people trembled after him. 8 And he tarried seven days, according to the set time that Samuel had appointed: but Samuel came not to Gilgal; and the people were scattered from him. 9 And Saul said, Bring hither a burnt offering to me, and peace offerings. And he offered the burnt offering.
